tagline: A sequence of love poems between a woman and a man, celebrating desire, delight, and faithful love, which Jews and Christians have also long read as a song of God's love for his people.
overview:
The Song of Songs is a book of poetry about love between a woman and a man. There is no law in it, no prophecy, no history of kings and battles, and God's name does not clearly appear in it. Instead two lovers speak to each other and about each other: they long for each other when apart, search for each other through the city at night, praise each other's bodies in lavish images drawn from gardens, vineyards, mountains, spices, and jewels, and at last declare that love is as strong as death. A group the woman calls the daughters of Jerusalem listens in and sometimes answers. The woman speaks more of the lines than anyone else, and her voice, eager, frank, and unashamed, sets the tone of the whole book.

The title means the finest or greatest song, in the way that holy of holies means the most holy place. For most of its history the book was read by Jews and Christians alike as an allegory: in the synagogue, a song of the love between God and Israel; in the church, a song of Christ and the church or Christ and the individual soul. Since the nineteenth century most interpreters have read it first as what it plainly appears to be, poetry celebrating human love and sexual desire within a committed bond. Many readers today hold both together, reading the Song as a celebration of married love that also, by its place in Scripture, points beyond itself to the love of God.

The Song matters because it refuses to treat the body and desire as shameful or merely useful. It sits in the Bible as a witness that the love of a man and a woman is God's good gift, worth singing about, and also as a warning that love is a fire too strong to be stirred up carelessly. Readers who have been taught only silence or suspicion about sexuality often find it startling. Readers who have been taught that desire is the whole of life find it just as startling, because it binds desire to faithfulness.
author:
The first verse reads “This is Solomon’s Song of Songs.” The Hebrew phrase can mean a song by Solomon, but it can also mean a song for, about, or dedicated to Solomon, and the same construction in the Psalms (for David) is debated in the same way. Jewish and Christian tradition generally took Solomon as the author. First Kings 4:32-33 says that Solomon composed 1,005 songs and speaks of his knowledge of plants and animals, which fits the Song's rich world of trees, flowers, and creatures. Solomon is named several times in the book (1:5; 3:7, 9, 11; 8:11-12), and a king appears in 1:4, 1:12, and 7:5.

Many scholars, including some conservative ones, think Solomon is a figure within the poems rather than their author. They note that he is sometimes spoken of from the outside, and in 8:11-12 his wealth seems to be set aside in favor of the woman's own freely given love. On this view an unnamed poet, or a collector of love poems, used the famous king as a symbol of splendor and romance. Others read the royal references as a genuine sign of Solomonic origin or of composition in his court. The book does not settle the question, and its meaning does not depend on it.
date: Those who hold to Solomonic authorship place the Song in the tenth century BC. Many modern scholars date its final form later, in the Persian period (fifth or fourth century BC) or the early Greek period, pointing to its Hebrew: it uses a short form of the relative word that is more common in later Hebrew, some forms resembling Aramaic, and what looks like a Persian loanword, pardes, orchard (4:13), the word behind the English paradise. Others answer that these features may reflect the dialect of northern Israel or the conventions of love poetry rather than a late date, and they note that the mention of Tirzah alongside Jerusalem (6:4) makes most sense before about 880 BC, when Tirzah was still a royal city of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:23-24). Some think the book gathers older poems that were edited over time. The range of proposals runs from the tenth to the third century BC.
setting:
The Song moves between two worlds. One is the countryside of Israel: vineyards and orchards, flocks of goats and sheep, gazelles and deer on the hills, spring rains and blossoming vines, and places from the far north (Lebanon, Hermon, Gilead) to the oasis of En-gedi by the Dead Sea. The other is the city and the royal court of Jerusalem, with its streets and watchmen, its walls and towers, its perfumes, gold, ivory, and purple cloth. The lovers move freely between these worlds, and the poems use both to praise each other.

Ancient Israel's neighbors also wrote love poetry. The closest parallels are Egyptian love songs from the New Kingdom period (roughly 1300 to 1100 BC), preserved on papyri and pottery, in which the lovers call each other brother and sister, praise each other's bodies, and complain of lovesickness, all as the Song does. Mesopotamian texts also contain love poetry, some of it tied to the worship of gods and goddesses. An older theory that the Song began as a pagan fertility liturgy has found little support. What sets the Song apart is its setting within Israel's faith, where love and marriage belong to the good order of creation rather than to the service of fertility gods.
purpose: Read as love poetry, the Song celebrates the goodness of desire and delight between a man and a woman, teaches the power of love and the need to guard it until its time, and honors a love that is mutual, exclusive, and lasting. It gives God's people words for a part of life that Scripture elsewhere often mentions only in warnings. Read as the synagogue and the church read it for centuries, it also gives words for the longing of God's people for God and his delight in them. Jewish communities read the Song at Passover, the feast that remembers God's rescue of Israel from Egypt, as one of the five short books (the Megillot) read at the festivals. The Song gives no statement of purpose, so these purposes are inferred from what it says and from how it has been used.
story: The Song belongs to the Bible's wisdom and poetry books, alongside Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and Ecclesiastes, and in the Hebrew Bible it stands among the Writings. It follows naturally after Genesis 2, where God brings the woman to the man and they are naked and unashamed, and after Genesis 3, where that ease is broken. The Song pictures love in a garden again, with a freedom and joy that echo Eden. The prophets used marriage as a picture of God's covenant with Israel (Hosea 1 to 3, Isaiah 54 and 62, Ezekiel 16), and the New Testament carries that picture forward: Paul calls marriage a mystery that speaks of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31-32), and the Bible ends with the wedding supper of the Lamb and a bride prepared for her husband (Revelation 19 and 21).
christ: The New Testament never quotes the Song of Songs directly, so any link to Christ is drawn from the wider biblical theme of God as bridegroom rather than from a prediction in the book. That theme is strong: Jesus calls himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19-20), John the Baptist calls himself the bridegroom's friend (John 3:29), Paul reads marriage as a picture of Christ's self-giving love for the church (Ephesians 5:25-32), and Revelation closes with the marriage of the Lamb. The long Christian tradition, from Origen in the third century to Bernard of Clairvaux in the twelfth and many Puritan preachers later, read the Song as a portrait of Christ's love for the church and the believer's love for him. Readers who take the Song first as human love poetry often make a related point in a different way: a love that is exclusive, self-giving, and as strong as death (8:6) is itself a reflection of the love God shows in Christ, and every faithful marriage is meant to be a small picture of it.
reading:
Read the Song as poetry, not as a story with a clear plot or a manual with rules. Its images are meant to evoke feeling and beauty, not to be pictured literally: when he says her hair is like a flock of goats streaming down Mount Gilead, he means the dark, rippling movement of her hair, not the look of goats. Watch who is speaking, which the Hebrew often marks by whether a word is masculine or feminine; many translations add headings for the woman, the man, and the friends, but those headings are editorial guesses. Watch for the refrains: the charge not to awaken love until the time is right (2:7; 3:5; 8:4), the declarations of mutual belonging (2:16; 6:3; 7:10), and the scenes of seeking and finding.

Interpreters differ over how the poems fit together. Some read a loose story of courtship, wedding, and married life, with the wedding at the center (3:6-5:1). Some read two main characters, the woman and the man, who is pictured sometimes as a king and sometimes as a shepherd; others, following a view first proposed in the eighteenth century and popularized in the nineteenth, read three, with the woman remaining faithful to her shepherd lover while Solomon tries to win her. Still others read an anthology of separate love poems joined by shared imagery. The allegorical reading, the natural reading, and the combined reading are each held by faithful Jews and Christians. The frank language is part of the book's point; it speaks with adult tact, through images rather than explicit description, and a reader should neither be embarrassed by it nor make it cruder than it is.

structure.title: Title
structure.summary: The superscription names the book the Song of Songs, the finest of songs, and connects it with Solomon.

structure.title: Longing and first delight
structure.summary: The woman longs for her beloved, explains her sun-darkened skin, and the lovers trade praise until she rests in his embrace and gives the first charge not to awaken love too soon.

structure.title: The spring invitation and the night search
structure.summary: He comes leaping over the hills to call her away into the springtime; later she searches the city at night, finds him, and repeats the charge.

structure.title: The royal wedding
structure.summary: Solomon's wedding procession arrives, the man praises his bride from head to breast, calls her a locked garden, and at her invitation enters his garden.

structure.title: Absence and praise
structure.summary: She hesitates to open to him, he departs, and she searches and is beaten by the watchmen; asked what makes him special, she praises him from head to foot, and they are reunited.

structure.title: Admiration and invitation
structure.summary: He praises her again as unique among all women, and she invites him to the countryside and longs to love him openly.

structure.title: Love as strong as death
structure.summary: The climax declares love stronger than death and beyond price, followed by closing scenes about a little sister, Solomon's vineyard, and a final call to the beloved.

themes.title: Love and desire as God's good gift
themes.body: The Song celebrates physical beauty, attraction, and the delight of lovers in each other without embarrassment. Its gardens and vineyards echo Eden, where God made the man and the woman for each other and called his creation very good. The book assumes that sexual love, rightly ordered, belongs to that goodness and deserves to be sung.

themes.title: Mutuality
themes.body: The woman is no silent object. She speaks first and most, initiates, invites, and praises him as fully as he praises her. The refrains of belonging run both ways: “My beloved is mine and I am his” (2:16). In a world where marriage was often arranged around property and power, the Song pictures a love of two persons who choose each other.

themes.title: The right time
themes.body: Three times the woman charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to arouse or awaken love until the time is right. Love is powerful, and the Song treats it as something to be guarded as well as enjoyed. Much of the Christian and Jewish tradition has read this as a call to patience and chastity, keeping the full expression of love for its proper setting.

themes.title: Exclusive and faithful love
themes.body: The woman is a garden locked up and a fountain sealed (4:12), open to one lover alone, and she asks him to set her as a seal over his heart (8:6). Among sixty queens and eighty concubines, his dove is unique (6:8-9). The Song's love is not casual; it is jealous in the good sense, claiming and giving the whole person.

themes.title: Love stronger than death
themes.body: The climax (8:6-7) calls love as strong as death, a fire that many waters cannot quench and that no fortune can buy. Some readers hear in the Hebrew word for its flame a final syllable that may be a short form of God's name, though many take it as a way of saying the fiercest flame. Either way, the Song ends by claiming for love a strength and worth that point beyond the lovers themselves.

keyChapters.why: The opening longing, the woman's own voice, and the first images of vineyard, flock, and king set the world of the whole book.
The spring invitation, the refrain of mutual belonging, and the first charge not to awaken love until the time is right.
The groom's praise of his bride and the image of the locked garden, the heart of the wedding sequence.
The night of hesitation and loss, and the woman's great poem of praise for her beloved.
The climax: love as strong as death, which many waters cannot quench and no wealth can buy.

parts.h: The Song of Songs in a minute
parts.body:
The Song of Songs is the twenty-second book of the Bible. It has eight chapters, and it is a book of poetry about love between a woman and a man.

There is no law in it, no prophecy, no history of kings and battles, and God's name does not clearly appear. Instead two lovers speak to each other and about each other. They long for each other when apart, search for each other through the city at night, praise each other in rich pictures drawn from gardens, vineyards, mountains, spices and jewels, and at last declare that love is as strong as death. A group the woman calls the daughters of Jerusalem listens in and sometimes answers.

The woman speaks more of the lines than anyone else, and her voice, eager, frank and unashamed, sets the tone of the whole book. Three times she gives the same charge: ‘Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right’ (2:7).

For most of its history the Song was read by Jews and Christians alike as a picture of God's love for his people. Since the nineteenth century most interpreters have read it first as what it plainly appears to be, poetry celebrating human love within a committed bond. Many readers today hold both together. It sits in the Bible as a witness that the love of a man and a woman is God's good gift, worth singing about, and as a warning that love is a fire too strong to be stirred up carelessly.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
The Song belongs to the Bible's books of poetry and wisdom, with Job, Psalms, Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. In Christian Bibles it follows Ecclesiastes. In the Hebrew Bible it stands among the Writings, and it is one of the five short scrolls read at the festivals. Jewish communities read it at Passover, the feast that remembers God's rescue of Israel from Egypt.

It follows naturally after Genesis 2, where God brings the woman to the man: ‘And the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed’ (Genesis 2:25). It follows Genesis 3 too, where that ease is broken. The Song pictures love in a garden again, with a freedom and joy that echo Eden.

The prophets used marriage as a picture of God's covenant with Israel (Hosea 1 to 3; Isaiah 54 and 62; Ezekiel 16), and the New Testament carries the picture forward. That is part of why readers have heard more in the Song than human love, though the Song itself never says so.

The first verse reads ‘This is Solomon’s Song of Songs’ (1:1). The Hebrew phrase can mean a song by Solomon, but it can also mean a song for, about or dedicated to Solomon. The same construction in the Psalms, ‘for David’, is debated in the same way. The title, Song of Songs, means the finest song, the way holy of holies means the most holy place.

Jewish and Christian tradition generally took Solomon as the author. The Bible says he ‘composed three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered a thousand and five’ (1 Kings 4:32), and that he spoke of trees and animals, which fits the Song's rich world of plants and creatures. Solomon is named several times in the book (1:5; 3:7, 9, 11; 8:11-12).

Many scholars, including some conservative ones, think Solomon is a figure in the poems rather than their author. He is sometimes spoken of from the outside, and in 8:11-12 his wealth seems to be set aside in favor of the woman's freely given love. On that view an unnamed poet, or a collector of love poems, used the famous king as a picture of splendor and romance. Others read the royal references as a real sign of Solomon's authorship or of his court.

The dates follow. Those who hold to Solomon's authorship place the Song in the tenth century BC. Many modern scholars date its final form later, in the Persian or early Greek period, pointing to its Hebrew, which includes what looks like a Persian loanword, pardes, orchard (4:13). Others answer that these features may reflect northern Israel's dialect or the conventions of love poetry. They note that naming Tirzah beside Jerusalem (6:4) makes most sense before about 880 BC, while Tirzah was still a royal city of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:23-24). Some think the book gathers older poems edited over time. The proposals run from the tenth to the third century BC. The book does not settle the question, its meaning does not depend on it, and these notes take no side.

parts.h: Human love, God's love, or both
parts.body:
How to read the Song is the oldest question about it, and serious readers have answered it in three main ways.

The allegorical reading was dominant in synagogue and church for many centuries. In the Targum and the rabbinic midrash the Song pictures the love between God and Israel. According to the Mishnah, Rabbi Akiva, in the early second century AD, insisted that it was the holiest of the Writings. In the church, from Origen in the third century to Bernard of Clairvaux in the twelfth and many Puritan preachers later, it pictured Christ and the church, or Christ and the believer's soul. Its strength is the Bible's frequent use of marriage for God's covenant. Its weakness is that the details often became arbitrary, with every image given a spiritual meaning.

The natural reading, now the most common among scholars, treats the Song as love poetry celebrating human desire and faithful love. Its strength is that it lets the text say what it plainly says.

A third reading tries to hold both together. The Song is first about human love, and because marriage is itself meant to picture God's covenant love, the Song can also point beyond itself.

Each of these readings is held by faithful Jews and Christians. These notes take no side. On any of them, the book's place in Scripture says that God cares about love between a man and a woman.

The Song is a conversation, and it helps to know who is talking. Hebrew often shows it by whether a word is masculine or feminine. Many translations add headings for the woman, the man and the friends, but those headings are editorial guesses, not part of the text.

The woman speaks first and most. She initiates, invites, searches and praises him as fully as he praises her. In a world where marriage was often arranged around property and power, the Song pictures two people who choose each other. Their refrain of belonging runs both ways: ‘My beloved is mine and I am his’ (2:16).

Interpreters differ over how many main characters there are. Some read two, the woman and the man, who is pictured sometimes as a king and sometimes as a shepherd. Others, following a view first proposed in the eighteenth century and made popular in the nineteenth, read three: the woman stays faithful to her shepherd lover while Solomon tries to win her. Still others read an anthology of separate love poems joined by shared images.

The daughters of Jerusalem are a group of women who listen, ask questions and receive the woman's charges.

Interpreters differ over how the poems fit together. Some read a loose story of courtship, wedding and married life, with the wedding at the center. Others read a collection of poems. Either way, the book moves through recognizable scenes.

The title (1:1) is followed by longing and first delight (1:2 to 2:7), ending in the first charge. Then come the spring invitation and the night search (2:8 to 3:5), ending in the second charge. At the center is a royal wedding (3:6 to 5:1): a procession, the man's praise of his bride, the locked garden, and her invitation. Then absence and praise (5:2 to 6:3): she hesitates, he is gone, she searches and is beaten by the watchmen, and she praises him from head to foot until they are together again. Then admiration and invitation (6:4 to 8:4), ending in the third charge. The climax comes last (8:5-14): love as strong as death, a little sister, Solomon's vineyard and a final call.

Watch for the refrains: the charge not to awaken love until the time is right (2:7; 3:5; 8:4), the words of mutual belonging (2:16; 6:3; 7:10), and the scenes of seeking and finding.

The Song opens in the woman's voice, full of longing: ‘For your love is more delightful than wine’ (1:2). She asks to be taken away with him, and the daughters of Jerusalem join in praise.

Then she speaks of herself. ‘I am dark, yet lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem’ (1:5). The small Hebrew word between dark and lovely can mean and or but. She means skin darkened by the sun from work outdoors, not her people or race. Her skin has been darkened, because her brothers were angry with her and made her keep the vineyards, so she could not keep her own (1:6). In a world where pale skin marked those who did not have to work outside, she defends her beauty without apology. She is not ashamed of the marks of her labor.

The lovers trade praise. His name for her, darling, is a word related to friend or companion. She asks where he grazes his flock at noon, so that she will not have to search for him. The section ends in his embrace and the first charge to the daughters of Jerusalem: do not stir up love until the time is right.

parts.h: Spring, and a search by night
parts.body:
In chapter 2 he comes leaping over the hills like a gazelle, stands at her window and calls her out into the spring: ‘For now the winter is past; the rain is over and gone. The flowers have appeared in the countryside; the season of singing has come’ (2:11-12). She asks him to catch the little foxes that spoil the vineyards, and says, ‘My beloved is mine and I am his’ (2:16).

In chapter 3 she searches for him at night. ‘On my bed at night I sought the one I love; I sought him, but did not find him’ (3:1). She goes through the streets and squares, asks the watchmen, and finds him just beyond them. Many readers take this scene as a dream or a picture of longing. The section ends with the second charge.

The Song is honest that love includes absence, searching and the fear of loss, not only delight.

parts.h: The wedding, and a garden locked up
parts.body:
At the center of the book is a wedding. A procession comes up from the wilderness: Solomon's carriage, guarded by sixty warriors, made of cedar and silver and gold. The daughters of Zion are called to see the king ‘wearing the crown his mother bestowed on the day of his wedding’ (3:11).

In chapter 4 the man praises his bride from head to heart in pictures drawn from the land: doves, flocks of goats, pomegranates, a tower, two fawns. The language is restrained and poetic. It uses images rather than explicit description, and it treats the body with admiration rather than crudeness. He calls her ‘my sister, my bride’, the language of family closeness and of marriage together.

‘My sister, my bride, you are a garden locked up, a spring enclosed, a fountain sealed’ (4:12). The picture is of a love kept for one person. Then she gives the invitation: ‘Let my beloved come into his garden’ (4:16). And he answers, ‘I have come to my garden, my sister, my bride’ (5:1).

The Song speaks of married love with joy and with tact. It is neither coy nor coarse. It is grateful.

Chapter 5 turns from union to loss. She is asleep but her heart is awake, and he knocks. She hesitates, then rises to open the door, ‘but he had turned and gone’ (5:6). She searches the city and calls, and he does not answer.

Then comes the book's hardest scene: ‘I encountered the watchmen on their rounds of the city. They beat me and bruised me; they took away my cloak, those guardians of the walls’ (5:7). Many readers take the scene as a dream, since it begins with her asleep, and hear in it the pain of separation. Others read it as a real event: a woman alone in the streets at night was in danger, and the watchmen's violence is an injustice the text records without approving. Older allegorical readers took the watchmen as leaders or trials that wound the soul seeking God. The Song does not explain the scene. It gives no warrant for violence against anyone, and the woman's love survives it.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Asked what makes her beloved better than others, she answers with a poem of praise from head to foot, and ends, ‘This is my beloved, and this is my friend’ (5:16). By chapter 6 they belong to each other again: ‘I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me’ (6:3).

parts.h: The right time, and love freely given
parts.body:
Three times the woman charges the daughters of Jerusalem: ‘Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right’ (2:7; 3:5; 8:4). Each time it comes after a moment of closeness.

Many readers, Jewish and Christian, have taken the charge as a call to patience and chastity: love has great power, and its full expression belongs to the right time and setting, which the Song and the rest of Scripture place in marriage. Others read the Hebrew as until it pleases, a request not to disturb the lovers. Still others hear general wisdom about love's power: it should not be forced, manipulated or stirred up artificially. These readings are not exclusive.

What the Song shows on every page is love given freely by both. The woman is not ashamed of desire, and her beloved never takes her against her will. The refrains of belonging run both ways. Nothing in the Song gives anyone a right to pressure, push or force another person. Love that is coerced is not the love this book sings.

The climax comes near the end: ‘Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm. For love is as strong as death, its jealousy as unrelenting as Sheol. Its sparks are fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all’ (8:6). ‘Mighty waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away’ (8:7), and no fortune can buy it.

A seal was a personal stamp worn on a cord or ring, used to sign and protect what belonged to someone. She asks to be his in that close, binding way. The word for jealousy here, qin'ah, means zeal, a fierce love that will not share its beloved.

The Hebrew word for the flame ends with a syllable, -yah, that may be a short form of God's name, though many take it as a way of saying the fiercest flame. Either way, the Song ends by claiming for love a strength and worth that point beyond the lovers.

The last scenes are puzzling and lovely: brothers deciding how to protect a little sister, Solomon's great vineyard set beside the woman's own, ‘But my own vineyard is mine to give’ (8:12), and a final call to the beloved to come quickly.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads the Song
parts.body:
The New Testament never quotes the Song of Songs directly. So any link to Christ comes from the wider biblical picture of God as bridegroom, not from a prediction in the book.

That picture is strong. Jesus calls himself the bridegroom: “How can the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?” (Mark 2:19). John the Baptist calls himself the bridegroom's friend (John 3:29). Paul reads marriage as a picture of Christ's love for the church: ‘This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church’ (Ephesians 5:32). And Revelation closes with the marriage of the Lamb and a bride made ready (Revelation 19:7).

Readers who take the Song first as human love poetry often make a related point in their own way: a love that is exclusive, self-giving and as strong as death is itself a reflection of the love God shows in Christ, and every faithful marriage is meant to be a small picture of it.

These notes keep to the lines the site's book page already draws, and add no others.

Read the Song as poetry, not as a story with a clear plot or a manual with rules. Its pictures are meant to stir feeling and beauty, not to be imagined literally. When he says her hair is like a flock of goats streaming down Mount Gilead, he means the dark, rippling movement of her hair, not the look of goats.

Watch who is speaking, and watch for the refrains: the charge about the right time, the words of mutual belonging, the seeking and the finding.

Read it with reverence and without embarrassment. The frank language is part of the book's point. It speaks with adult tact, through images, and a reader should neither be ashamed of it nor make it cruder than it is.

And read it with whatever reading you find truest, allegorical, natural or both, knowing that faithful readers have held each. On any of them the Song says that love between a man and a woman is a good gift from God, to be guarded and given freely, and stronger than death.

hard.line: A book of romantic love in the Bible: read as God's love, as human love God made good, or as both, by faithful readers in every age.
‘I am dark, yet lovely’. Darkened by work in the sun, she defends her beauty without apology.
Do not awaken love until the time is right: patience and chastity, love left undisturbed, or love never forced, and readings that can stand together.
A search through the city at night: often read as a dream of longing, honest that love includes absence and fear of loss.
Is the man Solomon? Read as Solomon himself, as a rival to a shepherd lover, or as a royal picture of how a wedding feels.
The groom's praise of his bride: restrained images, not explicit description, and the body honored as God's good gift.
A garden locked up: a love kept for one person, given freely by her own invitation (4:16).
The watchmen beat her: a dream of loss or a real injustice recorded without approval. No warrant for violence, and her love survives.
Sixty queens and eighty concubines: set aside, as the beloved is called unique, one above all.
Come back, O Shulammite: the woman's first title, found only here, read as a woman of Shunem, a feminine of Solomon, or a name of peace.
Frank physical imagery, veiled and figurative, to be received with reverence, not hidden from or made crude.
Love as strong as death, and a flame that may carry a short form of God's name, or simply mean the fiercest flame.
The little sister: brothers plan to protect her, and she answers in her own voice that she is a wall, at peace.
Solomon's vineyard and her own: wealth set beside a love that is hers to give.

words.line: Love, often in the plural for expressions of love, and also beloved, her name for him throughout (1:2; 2:16).
Love: the love the woman charges the daughters not to awaken before its time (2:7), strong as death (8:6).
Darling: a word related to friend or companion, his name for her (1:9).
Bride: the name he gives her at the center of the book (4:8-12; 5:1).
Sister: a word of family closeness, used with ‘bride’ in the love language of the ancient world (4:9).
Garden: the locked garden of 4:12 and the garden she invites him into, echoing Eden (4:16).
To rouse or awaken: the verb of the charge, do not awaken love until the time is right (2:7).
Banner or standard. ‘His banner over me is love’ (2:4).
Fox or jackal: the little foxes that spoil the vineyards in bloom (2:15).
The title given to the woman, found only here in the Bible (6:13).
Complete or perfect: ‘my perfect one’, one of a kind among many (6:9).
Desire or longing: ‘his desire is for me’ (7:10), the word used in Genesis 3:16.
Seal or signet, the personal stamp worn at the heart or on the arm (8:6).
Jealousy or zeal: a fierce love that will not share its beloved, unrelenting as Sheol (8:6).
Orchard, a loanword from Persian, the word behind the English ‘paradise’ (4:13).

timeline.what: Egyptian love songs are written on papyri and pottery, in which lovers call each other brother and sister and praise each other, as the Song does.
Solomon reigns. He is remembered for a thousand and five songs and for his knowledge of plants and animals (1 Kings 4:32-33).

timeline.when: The tenth century BC, on one view
timeline.what: If Solomon wrote the Song, or it comes from his court, it dates from his reign.
Tirzah is still a royal city of the northern kingdom; Omri reigns there before building Samaria (1 Kings 16:23-24). The Song names Tirzah beside Jerusalem (6:4).

timeline.when: The 400s to 200s BC, on another view
timeline.what: Many modern scholars date the Song's final form to the Persian or early Greek period, pointing to its Hebrew.
According to the Mishnah, Rabbi Akiva calls the Song the holiest of the Writings.
Origen reads the Song as a portrait of Christ's love for the church and the soul.
Bernard of Clairvaux preaches on the Song in the same tradition.
A three-character reading is first proposed: the woman, her shepherd lover and Solomon as a rival. It becomes popular in the nineteenth.
Most interpreters come to read the Song first as poetry of human love; many hold that reading together with the older one.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: Home of the daughters of Jerusalem, who listen and answer, and the city the beloved is compared to: ‘as lovely as Jerusalem’ (6:4).

places.name: Gilead
places.line: The hill country east of the Jordan, placed roughly. Her hair is ‘like a flock of goats streaming down Mount Gilead’ (4:1).

places.name: Damascus
places.line: The city to the north that a tower of Lebanon faces, in his praise of her (7:4).

teaching.mapNote: The Song names many places in pictures of beauty: Lebanon, Hermon, Amana and Senir in the north, En-gedi by the Dead Sea, Sharon, Carmel, Tirzah, Heshbon, Kedar and others. Only Jerusalem, Gilead and Damascus are placed in this site's records, so only they are drawn, Gilead roughly, as a region. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
